analysis.one_liner: Restricts insurers' prior-approval requirements in Medicare Advantage and forces faster, electronic decisions.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to cut Medicare Advantage prior-authorization delays won support from 280 House members of both parties, but died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Medicare Advantage plans — private insurance plans that about a third of Medicare beneficiaries choose instead of traditional Medicare — routinely require doctors to get approval before providing care. This bill would ban plans from adding new approval requirements mid-surgery, force plans to build an electronic system that answers routine requests in real time, and make plans publish each year how many requests they approve, deny, and lose on appeal, along with how long decisions take. The Health Department would set additional standards through formal rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans, who can face treatment delays while their plan decides whether to approve care. Their doctors and hospitals also benefit: they would spend less time chasing approvals and get faster answers on routine requests.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare Advantage enrollees and their doctors

how_it_helps.text: Medicare Advantage plans could not impose new prior-authorization requirements on surgical or invasive procedures furnished during a procedure for which approval was already given or not needed.

Plans would have to set up an electronic prior-authorization program that provides real-time decisions for items and services that are routinely approved, meeting technical standards set by the Health Department.

Plans would have to publish annually on a public website the percentage of requests approved, the percentage denied and later overturned on appeal, and the average and median time to a decision for each service.

The Health Department would set rules requiring plans to make timely determinations, explain denials, have requests reviewed by qualified medical personnel, and protect continuity of care for patients moving between plans.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare Advantage insurers, who would build new electronic systems and publish performance data. Insurers often argue prior authorization saves money by discouraging unnecessary care, so some of that cost could show up as higher premiums or richer limits on benefits; the bill has no direct government spending.

drawbacks.text: The bill's own findings acknowledge prior authorization is a tool to prevent unnecessary and unsafe care, so removing approval requirements mid-procedure removes some of that check.
Compliance costs fall on insurers, who could pass them to enrollees through premiums or reduced extra benefits; the bill text contains no offset or spending limit.

Most of the substantive standards are left to Health Department rulemaking, and plans can withhold criteria that disclose proprietary information, so the strength of the protections would depend on how a future administration writes the rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit to patients — fewer delays and less paperwork — is clear and the direct costs are administrative, borne mostly by insurers. The main honest concerns are that insurers might shift some costs into premiums and that the detail is left to regulators rather than written in the bill. On balance the bill is a targeted fix rather than a broad overhaul, and the bill itself preserves prior authorization as a legitimate tool.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees from its referral in June 2019 until the Congress ended in January 2021, with no markup or floor vote ever scheduled.

narrative.text: Representative Suzan DelBene introduced the bill on June 5, 2019 with Representatives Mike Kelly of Pennsylvania, Roger Marshall of Kansas, and Ami Bera of California, a mixed-party group of four members.
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee, and the next day it went to the Health Subcommittee.
Over the following nineteen months, the record shows no further action: no committee vote, no floor vote, and no companion step.

By the time the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, the bill had attracted 280 cosponsors — 143 of 231 House Democrats and 137 of 197 House Republicans — far more than the 218 needed to pass the House if it ever reached the floor.

Because the bill never received a vote, the House never adopted the requirement that Medicare Advantage plans publish their approval rates and response times, so plans continued to operate under the pre-2019 rules.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Medicare Advantage insurers came out ahead: they avoided the new electronic approval systems, mandatory public reporting of denial and appeal rates, and limits on mid-surgery authorization requirements. Patients who would have gained faster care are worse off.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship split almost evenly across parties — 143 of 231 Democrats and 137 of 197 Republicans cosigned — and the bill's four introducers included two Republicans; the opposition that mattered came from committee leadership, not from either party's rank and file.

industries.note: The bill would bar plans from adding new approval requirements mid-surgery, force real-time electronic decisions on routine requests, and publish their approval and appeal-overnight rates annually. Prior authorization is a tool insurers use to delay or deter expensive care, so the bill directly limits their control over seniors' care decisions.

Providers spend large amounts of staff time submitting prior authorization requests and would get an electronic system with real-time answers on routine requests and published insurer criteria. Faster approvals also mean fewer treatment delays for their patients.

industries.industry: Health information technology and EHR vendors
industries.note: The bill requires every Medicare Advantage plan to adopt standardized electronic prior authorization, integrated with electronic health records, creating mandated demand for software that connects plans and providers.
